1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Rubinstein System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3.background: Named after Akiba Rubinstein. Svetozar Gligorić and Lajos Portisch contributed greatly to its theory and practice at top level during their careers.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Normal Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O.strategy: The most common reply: Black castles, a move it will want in any case, and keeps the structure open. Black waits to see where White puts the bishop and knights before deciding between a central pawn strike and taking on c3.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 c5.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Rubinstein System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 c5.strategy: Presses on d4 immediately and keeps the central pawn set-up flexible. The threat to double White's pawns is held in reserve, so White has time to arrange to recapture with a piece, at the cost of a less natural development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: St. Petersburg Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop to tighten the grip on e4, in the spirit of the whole defence: the knight, the pin and the long diagonal all aim at that square. Black delays castling and the central pawns, so White gets time to choose a set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Nc6.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Rubinstein System, Taimanov Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Nc6.background: Named after Mark Taimanov. The young Bobby Fischer tried it several times, and Nukhim Rashkovsky has long favoured it.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queenside knight to prepare a pawn on e5 instead of waiting. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so the pressure on d4 now comes from a piece, and Black gives up some of the usual flexibility for an early fight over the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Ne4.strategy: Puts the knight on the central outpost at once to challenge the c3 knight, but Qc2 attacks it while guarding c3, so Black soon has to trade or retreat. White is left with a free hand in the centre, and Black has spent two moves with the same knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Bd3.strategy: White's most direct development: the bishop contests e4, the key square of the line, and looks towards the kingside. It keeps the knight on g1 undecided, and White accepts doubled pawns if Black takes on c3, in return for the bishop pair.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Ne2.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: St. Petersburg Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Ne2.strategy: Prepares to recapture on c3 with the knight, so Black's capture would no longer double the pawns and the main point of the pin is blunted. The price is a passive knight that blocks the king's bishop, which has to find another route.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight first and keeps the choice of where the king's bishop and the other pieces go. It usually leads to the same positions as the bishop move, with White fighting for e4 with pieces and accepting doubled pawns for the bishop pair.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Bd3.strategy: The point of the previous move: the bishop joins the knight in watching e4 along the long diagonal and also hits the g2 pawn, which has no defender. White has to answer that threat, so Black's set-up costs nothing in time.

Castles before the bishop commits, so the king is safe whichever set-up Black chooses. The game usually reaches the same fianchetto structure by transposition, but White is not forced to block the long diagonal and can choose a plan first.

Strikes at d4 at once, before the queen's bishop is developed. It keeps the centre tense, but White can release the tension or cramp Black with d5, and the light-squared bishop still has to find its place.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Bd3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: St. Petersburg Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Bd3.strategy: Develops a piece and blocks the long diagonal, so the g2 pawn is no longer attacked. White prepares to castle and keeps the choice between accepting doubled pawns and defending the centre with pieces.

Shuts the long diagonal with a pawn rather than a piece and prepares e4 to build a broad centre. The price is a looser king's side and a knight that loses its natural square on f3, so Black can strike at the centre while White is still unfolding.

Develops and covers c3 but ignores the attack on g2. Black can take the pawn, and White's rook has to go to the g-file to win a pawn back on g7, a risky way to start while the king is still in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Bd3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: St. Petersburg Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Bd3.strategy: Completes the kingside development and leaves the central plan open: Black can still choose between a solid pawn centre and a strike at d4. White usually keeps a slight initiative for a time, but Black generally equalises.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Bd3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: St. Petersburg Variation, with Ne4
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Bd3.background: So called because Black usually follows with 7...f5, giving a position that resembles the Dutch Defence. It is not a very common line.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Bd3.strategy: Heads straight for the outpost, with the knight backed by the bishop on b7. It challenges the white bishop at once, but the king stays in the centre and White gets good chances with a central pawn sacrifice that opens lines for the bishops.

Gives up the dark-squared bishop at once to double White's pawns, aiming for a closed centre where the knights outplay the bishops. The trade is a concession: White gets the bishop pair and the half-open b-file, and Black's king is still in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Ne2.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: St. Petersburg Variation, Fischer Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Ne2.background: Keres, Bronstein and Smyslov were early contributors to the theory of this line, and Bobby Fischer used it several times successfully.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Ne2.strategy: Attacks the c4 pawn, which has lost its defender because the knight blocks the king's bishop, and aims to trade the light-squared bishops so Black can play on the light squares. White has to protect the pawn or give it up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Ne2.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: St. Petersburg Variation, American Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Ne2.background: A name coined by Carsten Hansen, because the line was pioneered by Isaac Kashdan and then developed by Bisguier, Anthony Santasiere and Nick de Firmian.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Ne2.strategy: Occupies e4 at once, aims to trade off two minor pieces and then holds the square with a pawn on f5. The plan simplifies the game and rests entirely on control of the key square.

Hits d4 and keeps the pin alive: if White asks the bishop to decide, it can retreat along the diagonal instead of trading. Black keeps the tension on the queenside and the centre without committing the bishop's fate.

Puts the question to the bishop: with the knight ready to recapture on c3, White can afford it. The bishop must either trade for the knight without doubling the pawns or retreat, and White gains queenside space.

Gains space by pushing past the c5 pawn and cramps Black's pieces. White gives up the tension in the centre for a pawn on d5 that Black can challenge, so this is a plan of space against quick development.

Resolves the tension by capturing on c5, but Black recaptures with a pawn or the bishop and is comfortable at once. White has given up the pawn on d4, which held the centre and the e5 square, in exchange for nothing concrete.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Ne2.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: St. Petersburg Variation, Romanishin-Psakhis Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Ne2.background: Named by Carsten Hansen after Oleg Romanishin and Lev Psakhis, the two grandmasters primarily responsible for reviving the line and giving it new ideas.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6 5.Ne2.strategy: Keeps the bishop and the pin on c3 rather than trading, and invites White to try to trap it with a queenside pawn push. That attempt rarely works for White, since the c-pawn can strike back at the advancing pawns.

Settles the question of the bishop at once by trading it for the knight. White recaptures with the other knight, so the pawns stay healthy, and gets the bishop pair. A sound simplification: Black plays for control of e4 and a central strike, with no structural gain to show for the concession.

Releases the centre and lets White take the bishop, which Black repays by capturing the knight on c3. Material is level, but White keeps the bishop pair and a pawn on b4 that gains space, so Black has given up the point of the pin for little.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 c5 5.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop to its best square, where it helps control e4, and leaves the tension on d4 unresolved. White accepts doubled pawns if Black takes on c3, in return for the bishop pair and a flexible centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 c5 5.Ne2.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Rubinstein System, Rubinstein Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 c5 5.Ne2.strategy: Prevents Black from doubling the pawns by preparing to recapture on c3 with the knight. White keeps a healthy structure and can answer a pawn exchange in the centre with a recapture by the e-pawn, at the cost of a knight that blocks the king's bishop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 c5 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and covers d4 and e5, committing nothing about the bishop on f1 or the knight on c3. White accepts that ...Bxc3 may double the pawns in return for the bishop pair, and the game often merges with the lines that begin with Bd3.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 c5 5.Bd3.strategy: Develops a piece and adds a second attacker to d4. Black keeps the option of taking on c3 at once and building a closed position, in which the knights are better placed than White's bishops and the doubled pawns leave White without queenside breaks.

Challenges the centre from both sides before developing, and the pin on c3 matters here: the knight cannot take on d5. White can exchange or hold the tension, and Black has to complete development quickly once the centre opens.

Castles first, putting the king safe before the centre opens and keeping both the central strike with the d-pawn and the development of the queen's knight in reserve. It is the most flexible treatment, though White chooses the set-up before Black has shown a plan.

The flexible developing move: it covers d4 and e5 and lets White meet ...Bxc3 with the bishop pair and doubled c-pawns, without a tempo spent on a3. White bets that the two bishops and the centre outweigh the weak queenside pawns once the position opens.

Asks the bishop to decide at once, but Black was ready to take on c3 anyway. White gets the bishop pair and doubled c-pawns for a tempo spent on the a-pawn while the kingside is still undeveloped, so Black has time to set up a blockade.

With the bishop already on d3, the knight on e2 does not block it. It guards c3 and d4, and answers ...Bxc3 with a recapture by the knight, so White keeps healthy pawns; the knight is passive, but the move order sidesteps the doubled pawns.
Takes the knight and doubles White's pawns, the usual aim of the pin. Black gives up the bishop pair for a lasting queenside weakness and keeps the pressure on d4 with the c-pawn and the knight.

Refuses the exchange and keeps the pin, but the bishop is stranded on the edge of the board. White can gain queenside space with a pawn push at the bishop, and Black has to find precise counterplay against the advancing pawns.

Opens the centre and lets White take the bishop, which Black repays by capturing the knight on c3. Material is level, but White keeps the bishop pair and a pawn on b4 that gains space; playable, yet it surrenders the pin.

Captures at once, without waiting for a3. Black then closes the centre and blockades the dark squares, so that the knights outplay White's bishops and the doubled c-pawns leave White without pawn breaks on the queenside.

Prepares ...e5 and a closed, dark-square blockade, where the knights outplay White's bishops. The bishop stays on b4 for now, but White can unpin with Bd2 and avoid the doubled pawns the blockade relies on.

Castles before committing the bishop or the centre pawns. The king is safe, and Black can still double White's pawns or strike at d4 on the next move; the price is that White also gets a free move to decide the set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 c5 5.Ne2.strategy: Releases the tension in the centre and clears c5, giving the bishop a retreat to e7. White recaptures with the e-pawn, because taking with the knight would let ...Bxc3+ double the pawns after all.

Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop and keeps the tension on d4 instead of releasing it. The bishop has a retreat on a5 if White asks it a question, and Black fights for e4 and the long diagonal.

Castles before committing, keeping the exchange on d4 and the bishop's retreats open. Safe and flexible, but White chooses when to release the tension or ask the bishop a question with a3, so Black reacts rather than sets the course.

Recaptures with the pawn so that the knight stays on e2 to guard c3. White gets a broad pawn centre on c4 and d4 and a free dark-squared bishop, but the knight is passive and the f1-bishop still has to find a way out.

Recaptures with the knight, but that knight was guarding c3: ...Bxc3+ now takes with check and bxc3 doubles White's pawns, the structure Ne2 was played to avoid. White keeps the bishop pair and an active knight, but the queenside is damaged.
Recaptures with the queen, which stands exposed on a central square: ...Nc6 attacks it at once, and Black gains time for development while the pin stays.

Castles first and does not push the d-pawn yet, which would allow White to gain space with c5. The bishop keeps its retreat to e7 in reserve, and a quiet game follows in which White's central pawns face Black's piece play.

Challenges the centre at once and invites White to gain queenside space with the c-pawn. Black neutralises the resulting pawn majority with play on the wing, while White uses a lead in development for the kingside; the game is sharper than after castling.
Develops with pressure on d4, but invites the pawn to d5, which chases the knight. Black keeps the structure sound, but loses time and delays castling, which White's central pawns can exploit.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Ne4 5.Qc.strategy: Attacks the undefended knight on e4; the pinned knight on c3 cannot take it, so the queen does the work. It also guards c3, which both the knight on e4 and the bishop attack.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Ne4 5.Bd.strategy: Breaks the pin so that the knight can take on e4, and offers to trade the bishop for Black's outpost knight. Solid but modest: the bishop that might otherwise watch the dark squares is exchanged, and Black keeps an easy game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Ne4 5.Ne.strategy: Leaves f2 short of defenders: ...Qh4 attacks it twice, with the queen and the knight on e4, and White's king alone guards it. The c3 knight is pinned and cannot take on e4, so White has no comfortable defence.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Ne4 5.Qc.strategy: Supports the knight with a pawn so that it can stay on e4, a bold way to hold the central square. The price is a looser king's side: the e8-h5 diagonal is open and e6 is weaker, with Black's king still uncastled.

Trades the outpost knight for the pinned one. White has to recapture with the pawn, because the queen would lose to the bishop, so the c-pawns are doubled and the pawn on c3 now attacks the bishop. Black gives up the strong knight but gets a lasting queenside weakness, while White's pawn centre grows.

Takes the knight first, so the doubled c-pawns cost Black the bishop pair, and must then hold the outpost, for instance with a pawn. The knight stays on e4, but White's two bishops and pawn centre give White the easier game.
Develops and covers e5 and d4, ready to challenge the outpost with the bishop. Black's knight now relies on the f5 pawn alone, so Black needs more support or has to trade it for the knight on c3.

Puts the question to the bishop. If it takes on c3, White has to recapture with the pawn, because the queen would fall to the knight on e4, so the c-pawns double in return for the bishop pair. White spends a tempo while Black keeps the outpost.

Breaks the pin so that the knight can take on e4, and offers to trade the bishop for the outpost knight. Solid but modest: the bishop is exchanged for a knight and White has made no progress against the outpost.
Prepares ...Bb7 to give the e4 knight a second defender. Black answers the challenge to the outpost by adding force to it rather than trading.

Trades the outpost knight for the pinned one. White recaptures with the pawn, which doubles the c-pawns and attacks the bishop; Black keeps both bishops and a clear target on the queenside. The price is the strong knight and the pin, and White's pawn centre is free to expand.
Castles first and leaves the knight on e4 relying on the f-pawn alone, which is risky: White can pile up on e4 or ask the bishop a question before ...b6 and ...Bb7 arrive to support it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Bd.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Normal Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Bd.strategy: The main line: the bishop takes charge of e4 and eyes the kingside, while the knight on g1 still has its choice of square. White keeps the option of allowing or avoiding doubled pawns, and Black has to commit to a plan in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Ne.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Reshevsky Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Ne.strategy: Makes sure a capture on c3 can be answered by the knight, so Black cannot double the pawns. The cost is time and coordination: the knight sits in front of the f1-bishop and has to find a better square, while Black can build the centre in peace.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Nf.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, covers d4 and e5 and leaves the f1-bishop's square undecided. White allows ...Bxc3 to double the pawns, counting on the bishop pair and the centre; Black can now take the centre with a pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.a3.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop at once: Black takes on c3, and White gets the bishop pair and a free hand in the centre for doubled c-pawns. Whether that is enough is the whole game, and White often cannot find the attack that makes up for the structure.
Takes at once: the bishop is attacked, and the exchange is the point of the defence. Black gives up the bishop pair to leave White with doubled c-pawns, a weakness to aim at for the rest of the game.
Keeps the pin and avoids the exchange, but White gains queenside space with a pawn push that drives the bishop back. Black has given up the idea of doubling White's pawns and lost time.
Retreats and keeps the bishop, a move that gives up the pin and a tempo. White gets a free hand in the centre and Black has to equalise with a central strike; solid, but passive.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.a3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Sämisch Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.a3.strategy: The only sound recapture: blocking the check or moving the king leaves White a piece down. White gets the bishop pair and a pawn mass on c3, c4, d4 and e3; the doubled pawn on c4 is the weakness Black will target, and White needs the attack to come before that pressure tells.
Blocks the check instead of retaking, so the knight is never won back: after ...Bxd2+ the bishops come off and White is a whole piece down.
Steps out of the check without retaking, so Black has simply won a knight. White has also given up castling and leaves the king in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Bd.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Normal Variation, Classical Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Bd.strategy: The classical reply: a pawn takes the centre and attacks c4, so White cannot play e4 undisturbed. Black's pawns on d5 and e6 form a sturdy centre and the pin on c3 stays. White must soon decide how to resolve the tension on c4.
Attacks d4 at once and keeps the d-pawn flexible, so Black decides the central structure later. White has to meet the pressure by developing quickly, and the game can still reach the main line.

Prepares the bishop on b7, which watches e4 and the central light squares from a distance, and leaves the choice of central pawn structure for later. The price is that White's centre goes unchallenged for now.
Develops, adds a defender to d4 and prepares to castle. White keeps the centre intact and leaves Black the next decision: how to use the pressure on d4 while the bishop still pins c3.

Prepares to retake on c3 with the knight, so the bishop's exchange no longer ruins White's pawns, while the bishop on d3 keeps its open diagonal. The knight is less active than on f3, but White keeps a sound structure and the bishop pair in reserve.

Takes the pawn, but ...Bxc5 regains it at once and the bishop is well placed on c5. White has traded its d-pawn for Black's c-pawn and given up the tension in the centre, so the move gains nothing and leaves Black comfortable.
Prepares ...Bb7, adding pressure on e4 and the central light squares, while the c5 pawn keeps working against d4. Black can trade on d4 later and play for activity against a possible isolated pawn.

The main line: the d-pawn claims a share of the centre and attacks c4, while the c-pawn already presses d4. White has to settle the tension soon, and Black reaches a well-trodden structure in which the pin stays and Black has an easy plan.

Adds a second attacker to d4 and develops the queen's knight, keeping the pin. Black is ready to trade the bishop for the knight and blockade the doubled pawns, aiming for a closed game in which Black's knights are better than White's bishops.
Develops the knight, covers d4 and e5 and prepares castling. White finishes development before resolving the tension on c4, d5 and c3, and Black has to choose a way to challenge the centre.
Forces the bishop to decide before White's knight is out. If Black takes on c3 and later on c4, the bishop retakes and the doubling disappears, leaving White a broad centre and the bishop pair.

Prepares to retake on c3 with the knight, so the pin loses its sting and White never has to accept doubled pawns. With the bishop already on d3 it is not boxed in by the knight. The knight stands less actively than on f3, and White has to watch the pressure on c4.

Removes the pawn that attacks c4 and clarifies the centre: after ...exd5 the pin stays, and White can bring the knight to e2 to retake on c3 without doubling the pawns. The price is the lost tension, and the game becomes slow and manoeuvring.
Takes the knight, doubling White's pawns at the price of the bishop pair. The c4 pawn, already attacked by the d-pawn, is the first target, and White has to be ready to undouble the pawns.

Declines the exchange and keeps the dark-squared bishop, accepting a more passive set-up. The pin on c3 ends, so White is free to open the centre with the c-pawn and play for a space edge, while Black's solid pawns on d5 and e6 and a safe king give a sound, if somewhat cramped, game.

Avoids the exchange and aims the bishop at the kingside, but it stands loosely on d6, where c4-c5 attacks it with tempo and gains queenside space. Black has to retreat, and White's space is the lasting gain.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Bd.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Normal Variation, Gligoric System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Bd.strategy: Attacks the base of White's centre and claims a share of it. This is the main line: both sides have developed naturally, and the fight is over who profits from the tensions on c4, d4 and c3.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Bd.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Normal Variation, Schlechter Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Bd.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 against e4 and keeps the structure compact. A solid set-up: White often holds the initiative early, but Black usually equalises in the end.
Attacks d4 with a piece, but the knight blocks the c-pawn, which can no longer challenge d4 itself. Black gets a sound but less direct set-up than the main line.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Ne.strategy: Takes the centre and attacks c4 while White's bishop is still shut in by the knight on e2. Black does not count on doubling White's pawns here, because the knight can recapture on c3; the fight is for the centre instead.

Attacks d4 at once and leaves the structure open, so Black decides the central pawns later. The knight on e2 already guards d4 and can retake on c3, so doubling White's pawns is not on offer; the fight is for the centre.

Prepares the bishop on b7 to watch the central light squares from a distance, but leaves the centre to White: a3 soon asks the bishop to decide, and the knight on e2 can retake on c3 without doubled pawns. A sound but slow set-up.
Puts the question to the bishop. Capturing on c3 would give up the bishop for a knight that Ne2 can retake, leaving White's pawns intact, so Black has to retreat and White is rid of the pin.

Releases the tension on c4 and takes away Black's pressure on it: after ...exd5 the centre is settled and the pin stays. The knight on e2 can still retake on c3 without doubling the pawns, so White gives up little and plays a slow game without weaknesses.

Gains queenside space and gives up the tension on c4, but it lets Black's knight settle on e4 and gives Black a free hand to strike back at d4 with the e-pawn. The structure is sound, and White keeps a small space edge.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Ne.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Simagin Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Ne.strategy: Keeps the bishop and points it at h2 on the diagonal towards White's kingside, instead of trading on c3, where the knight could recapture without doubled pawns. Black stays active and keeps the tension in the centre.

The main line: the bishop retreats to a safe, compact square instead of exchanging itself for a knight that the e2 knight can retake without doubling the pawns. Black keeps both bishops and a sound centre, and the game becomes a manoeuvring fight over the centre in which both sides are sound.

Gives up the bishop for a knight that Ne2 retakes without a doubled pawn, so Black gains nothing in structure and hands White the bishop pair. The position stays sound and the pressure on c4 persists, but Black has parted with its best minor piece for little.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Nf.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Normal Variation, Ragozin Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Nf.strategy: Builds a solid pawn centre on d5 and e6 and keeps the pin, so e4 is hard for White to push. White has to decide how to deal with the pin and the pressure on c4, while Black reaches a familiar structure with the bishop already active.

Presses on d4 at once and leaves the structure open, so Black can still decide whether to build a centre with the d-pawn or to trade on d4. White has to keep developing while the pin lasts, and the game often returns to the main line.

Prepares the bishop on b7, which adds pressure on e4 and the central light squares without committing a central pawn. Black keeps the pin and stays flexible, accepting that White gets time to finish development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Nf.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Normal Variation, Sämisch Deferred
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Nf.strategy: Forces the bishop to decide. If Black takes on c3, White accepts doubled pawns for the bishop pair and aims to cure the weakness by exchanging on d5 and to build the centre with the bishop pair behind it.
Breaks the pin, so ...Bxc3 no longer doubles the pawns. The price is a tempo and a passive dark-squared bishop on d2, which leaves Black free to put pressure on the c4 pawn and the centre.

The main line: the bishop takes its natural post on the b1-h7 diagonal, aiming at the kingside and ready to retake if Black captures on c4. White completes development before committing the centre, and the game heads for the long manoeuvring fight of the main line with the pin still on.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Nf.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Normal Variation, Ragozin Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O 5.Nf.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4 now that the pin is lifted and ...Bxc3 would not double any pawns. Black plays for piece activity and a central break, with the c4 pawn as a target.

Strikes at d4 while White's bishop sits passively on d2: the c-pawn attacks d4 and the d-pawn already presses c4, so White has to settle both tensions before finishing development. Black gets a share of the centre and easy development.

Takes the pawn at once; White regains it with Bxc4, which also develops the bishop. Black gives up the d5 pawn and its hold on e4, but the passive Bd2 has cost White time, so Black can strike back at the centre and develop freely.
